It is clear that the courts have a wide variety of procedures that can be followed and orders that can be made to prevent and stop litigation that is vexatious or an abuse of the process of the courts. Such litigation obviously has an adverse effect on the opposing party, but just as importantly, it has an adverse effect on the administration of justice by wasting valuable court time on unmeritorious litigation. The remedies available to the courts include the striking out of vexatious pleadings, the striking out of abusive proceedings, and, of course, the making of Isaac Wunder orders where there is repeated unmeritorious litigation by a party to proceedings. 

 135.           An Isaac Wunder order is to be made sparingly. Access to justice is an important constitutional right but nevertheless, in an appropriate case, there may be some restrictions on the right of access to the courts. Accordingly, an Isaac Wunder order will only be made after a number of unmeritorious applications have been made by the party concerned. The making of such an order does not preclude a party from enjoying their right of access to justice, given that the sole effect of such an order is to restrict such party from initiating a new application or proceedings without the leave of the court. As such, if the party concerned is in a position to establish grounds for bringing a further application, or issuing further proceedings, then that will be permitted. It must be borne in mind that an Isaac Wunder order is not made as a matter of routine. It is simply the requirement of a party to obtain leave of the Court (usually the President of the Court or a judge nominated by the President) before instituting fresh proceedings or application against a specific defendant. It is not a restriction on the issuing of proceedings in a statable case. If the case is unstateable, for example, because the points raised have already been considered and determined in earlier proceedings, leave will not be granted. There is nothing unusual about requiring a party to obtain leave of the court for certain types of proceedings such as most types of judicial review. It is a further procedural step that must be taken but that is as far as it goes. What has to be established before leave will be granted will be discussed below. 

 136.           There is no bar to making an Isaac Wunder order in family law proceedings. This was accepted on behalf of the appellant, and it has to be said, it would be somewhat surprising if any other view was expressed by the appellant, given that the suggestion of making such an order in these proceedings came from the appellant himself as an alternative to making an order for costs, as set out above. 

 137.           Family law proceedings can be, by their nature, the subject of multiple applications to the court, because certain orders made in such proceedings are not " final " orders, in the sense that orders in other types of proceedings can be said to be. For example, issues relating to maintenance can be re-opened where there has been a change of circumstances of one or other of the parties to such proceedings. Over the course of time, it would be surprising if certain types of orders in such proceedings did not have to be revisited. 

 138.           In the case of family law proceedings, the best interests of the child have to be taken into account before making an Isaac Wunder order concerning matters such as applications in relation to custody, access, or maintenance. There may be other areas of family law proceedings that also require the best interests of the child to be taken into account - this is not intended to be an exhaustive list of the areas in which these interests have to be considered. 

 139.           It should be borne in mind that in many cases, a child, while not a party to the proceedings, may be adversely affected by a constant series of applications, for example, in relation to custody/access. Repetitious applications which are unmeritorious will inevitably have the effect of causing increased disharmony and acrimony within the family setting, and have the potential to cause other problems, such as the expenditure of large sums of money on costs which would be better spent on the family as a whole. In particular, in the context of custody/access proceedings, the child may be required to undergo repeated psychological or similar assessments for the purpose of the proceedings. This is unlikely to be beneficial to the child. 

 140.           In considering whether to make an Isaac Wunder order, a court must act proportionately. 

 141.           The structured approach to the making of such orders advocated for on behalf of the appellant is something that could be considered by the legislature, and/or the Rules Committees of the courts, but there is nothing to suggest that the manner in which such orders now fall to be made gives rise to uncertainty or lack of clarity or proportionality as was suggested. Such orders are made in accordance with well-established case law. While from time to time, Rules of court are amended to reflect such well-established case law, as, for example, in the case of the recent amendment to O. 19, r. 28 of the RSC, the fact that no such change has been introduced for the making of Isaac Wunder orders does not present a difficulty to the making of such orders. The introduction of Rules or indeed Practice Directions to deal with such applications may be of assistance but, as of now, no specific problem has been shown to exist which would preclude the making of such orders. 

 142.           Finally, it should be observed that the making of such orders, being part of the inherent powers of the court to prevent an abuse of process, may not be confined to the High Court, the Court of Appeal, and the Supreme Court. Further, in principle, it appears that such orders can be made by the Circuit Court and the District Court despite some judicial pronouncements to the contrary but subject to certain limitations which are about to be discussed. 

 Courts of Local and Limited Jurisdiction 

 143.           The Circuit Court and District Court are courts of local and limited jurisdiction with a right of appeal as determined by law (see Article 34.3.4 ° of the Constitution). The precise extent of what is meant by "local and limited" need not be determined in these proceedings but, as Clarke C. J. observed in Permanent TSB v Langan [2018] 1 IR 375, the requirements of Article 34.3.4 must nonetheless be respected. Thus, assuming that these courts have jurisdiction to make Isaac Wunder orders, it would appear that some geographical or other limitation must necessarily apply in relation to the jurisdiction or venue in relation to which such orders may be made. Of course, the extent of the jurisdiction of the Circuit Court to make such orders gave rise to an issue in these proceedings. The order made in the Circuit Court herein precluded the appellant from taking any further proceedings in the District Court, Circuit Court, or, for that matter, any other court, without leave of the Circuit Court. As Simons J. said at para. 16 of his judgment herein: 

 "It is unnecessary, for the purpose of resolving the procedural objection raised in the present case, to determine whether the Circuit Court possesses its own independent jurisdiction to make a restraining order in respect of proceedings before it. Whatever the precise position may be in this regard, the Circuit Court most certainly does not have jurisdiction to impose a restriction in the right of access to the High Court. The High Court exercises a supervisory jurisdiction over the Circuit Court, by way of judicial review, and the Circuit Court cannot frustrate the exercise of that supervisory jurisdiction by purporting to oblige a party to obtain prior permission from the Circuit Court before having recourse to the High Court. If and insofar as the order of 23 May 2022 purports to impose such an obligation - and it is not apparent from the transcript that this is what the Circuit Court judge actually intended - this represents an error on the face of the record. This aspect of the order cannot oust the High Court's full original jurisdiction to entertain these judicial review proceedings." 

 144.           For the avoidance of doubt, I should add that as part of its supervisory role in relation to both the Circuit Court and the District Court, I see no reason why the High Court could not, in an appropriate case make an Isaac Wunder order in respect of proceedings in the Circuit Court and the District Court. Further, it seems to me that in an appropriate case, the High Court must have jurisdiction to injunct a party from commencing or continuing proceedings in the Circuit or District Court where those proceedings would amount to an abuse of process   Leaving aside the question of Isaac Wunder orders, it appears that the High Court apart from its supervisory role over the Circuit and Districts courts by means of judicial review has had a longstanding supervisory role in relation to some aspects case of contempt of court whereby the High Court has jurisdiction to punish parties for contempt of court occurring in the District and Circuit Court. This simply reflects the long-standing supervisory role of the High Court in respect of those courts. (For an interesting discussion on this issue, see the LRC Consultation Paper on Contempt (p.p. 182-184 and the cases of Attorney General v O'Ryan and Boyd [1947] IR 213 and AG v Connolly [1946] IR 82.) I have read the judgment of Murray J. where he deals with the supervisory role of the High Court and I agree with the views expressed therein. 

 145.           The Court of Appeal in its judgment in this matter did not deal with this aspect of the proceedings in any detail, saying simply at para. 6 of the second judgment as follows: 

 "The issue which then arose was whether that small outstanding balance of these proceedings (regarding the validity of the Isaac Wunder order made by the Circuit Court) should be remitted to the High Court for determination, in circumstances where the trial judge had cast doubt upon the validity of that order as made, and where remittal would, inevitably, give rise to further costs. The Court indicated to the parties that, in the alternative, this Court could make an order quashing the Isaac Wunder order and proceed to entertain an application by the applicant for a fresh Isaac Wunder order. The parties agreed to this course of action, and subsequently written submissions were filed and a supplemental hearing was held on this issue." 

 146.           It seems to me that the reasoning employed by Simons J. in para. 16 of his judgment set out above is correct. He was of the view that the Circuit Court does not have jurisdiction to make an order ousting the jurisdiction of the High Court, which has full original jurisdiction. That must be so and does not require further elaboration. 

 147.           That does not answer the question of whether the Circuit Court (and the District Court) has itself jurisdiction to make such orders. Overall, it appears to me that in circumstances where the making of an Isaac Wunder order is part of a court's panoply of powers to protect the administration of justice from an abuse of process, it would be difficult to see why the Circuit Court could not make such orders, if necessary and appropriate in the circumstances. Dealing with the jurisdiction of the Circuit Court, it will be noted that the Courts (Supplemental Provisions) Act 1961 ("the 1961 Act") and, in particular, s. 22(1)(a) provides: 

 " Subject to paragraphs (b) and (c) of this subsection, the Circuit Court shall, concurrently with the High Court, have all the jurisdiction of the High Court to hear and determine any proceedings of the kind mentioned in column (2) of the Third Schedule to this Act at any reference number ." 

 148.           While this section concerns the type of proceedings which can be heard by the Circuit Court (subject to quantitative limits), it is noteworthy that the Circuit Court has " all the jurisdiction of the High Court " to deal with such proceedings. It would also be worth mentioning the provisions of s. 22(6) of the 1961 Act. It provides as follows: 

 "The Circuit Court, as regards any cause of action for the time being within its jurisdiction , shall, in any proceedings before it- 

 (a)    Grant such relief, redress or remedy or combination of remedies, absolute or conditional, 

 (b)    Give such and the like effect to every round of defence or counterclaim, legal or equitable, 

 as ought to be granted or given in the like case by the High Court and in as full and ample a manner." 

 These specific provisions may lead to the view that,  bearing in mind that the High Court has jurisdiction to make such orders, it follows from the terms of s.22 (6) of the 1961 Act that the Circuit Court must also have the same jurisdiction and power to make an Isaac Wunder order, subject to any limits relating to the local and limited nature of the jurisdiction of the Circuit Court. While these are  important provisions in relation to the overall jurisdiction of the Circuit Court and  the manner in which it exercises its jurisdiction, I am satisfied that the Circuit Court, as a court established under the Constitution to administer the law, has an inherent power to make Isaac Wunder orders in order to protest the administration of justice  and is not reliant on the provisions of s. 22 (6) to do so. 

 149.           This is so notwithstanding the decision of the Court of Appeal in the case of Morgan v. The Labour Court & Ors [2025] IECA 2 referred to by the appellant. That was a case in which Isaac Wunder orders were made by the High Court following the hearing of a number of applications including appeals from the Labour Court. In the course of the hearing before the High Court, it was noted that the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) had a statutory power to strike out proceedings that were " frivolous or vexatious " but it had no jurisdiction to make an Isaac Wunder- type order . Whelan J., giving the judgment of the Court of Appeal, commented at para. 172 of her judgment: 

 "The WRC and the Labour Court, as creatures of statute, lack any inherent jurisdiction. The ambit of their respective powers is delineated by the relevant governing legislation." 

 150.           The issue at the heart of that case was the jurisdiction of the High Court to extend the ambit of the Isaac Wunder orders to cover proceedings before the WRC and the Labour Court, and it was concluded therein that there was such jurisdiction. 

 151.           The point was made therein that the power of those bodies, as creatures of statute, was delineated by the relevant governing legislation. That is undoubtedly so. The Circuit Court is also a creature of statute, albeit provided for by the Constitution as previously mentioned. However, having been established, it is a Court established under the Constitution engaged in the administration of justice. In the case of the Circuit Court, as I have explained above, the jurisdiction of the Circuit Court is sufficiently wide, in my view, to enable that Court to make Isaac Wunder orders  by reason of its inherent power.. It is not subject to the limitations applicable to the WRC and the Labour Court which are not courts established under the Constitution and whose jurisdiction is limited by statute to striking out frivolous or vexatious litigation. 

 152.           While the jurisdiction conferred on the District Court by the 1961 Act is set out in different terms and not expressed as being co-extensive with that of the High Court in the way that the Circuit Court is expressly stated to be (see s. 33 of the 1961 Act),  the Attorney General, in response to questions raised by the Court in this regard, made the point that the District and Circuit Courts are obliged to administer justice in compliance with the Constitution and such obligation is not affected by those courts being of local and limited jurisdiction. Reference was made to the decision in the case of The People v. Lynch [1982] I.R. 64 (at p. 84) where Walsh J explained: 

 "...the judges of the District Court and judges of the Circuit Court are not dispensed from, or expected to overlook, their constitutional obligation to uphold the constitution in the discharge of their constitutional and legal function of administering justice." 

 153.           Reference was also made to the comments of Geoghegan J. in Whelan v. Kirby [2004] IESC 17 , [2005] 2 IR 30 in which he observed: 

 "There is jurisdiction in the District Court to make any order that would be necessary for the fulfilment of the constitutional obligation of a fair trial and fair procedures." 

 154.           Thus, while the terms of the legislation conferring jurisdiction on the Circuit Court and the District Court are expressed differently, both courts are engaged in the process of the administration of justice. The jurisdiction of the District Court is less extensive than the Circuit Court, but nonetheless, it seems to me that the District Court, no less than any other Court, is entitled to ensure that proceedings before it are not used in such a way as to amount to an abuse of process. To refer back to the earlier discussion on inherent powers and inherent jurisdiction, it seems to me that every court has the power to regulate the proceedings before it, and this includes restricting proceedings which amount to an abuse of process. It would seem strange if the District Court was powerless in the face of an abuse of process to take any steps to prevent such abuse. The passages referred to from the Lynch case and Whelan v. Kirby above make it clear that both the Circuit Court and the District Court have obligations under the Constitution in relation to fair trials and fair procedures when engaged in the administration of justice. That obligation must include the possibility of restricting access to court when the proceedings constitute an abuse of process. In the circumstances, it seems to me that the powers of the District Court in exercising its jurisdiction encompass the inherent power of a court to make orders which are necessary to prevent an abuse of process. Thus, while I have referred above to the statutory provisions in relation to the jurisdiction of the Circuit Court, it seems to me that the important basis for the making of such orders  is the inherent power of a court engaged in the administration of justice to make an Isaac Wunder order when the administration of justice so requires. Accordingly, regardless of the differences in the terms of the legislation setting out the respective jurisdictions of the Circuit and District Court, both courts must have the same inherent power to make such orders as are necessary to ensure that the administration of justice in those courts is protected from abuse. 

 155.           It could, however, be argued that there is an issue as to the geographical limit of orders of the Circuit Court. In other words, can an order made by a Circuit judge sitting in the Dublin Circuit, for example, preclude an application being made to issue proceedings in another circuit of the Circuit Court? There is an interesting discussion of the local and limited jurisdiction of the Circuit Court to be found in the case of Permanent TSB plc v Langan [2017] IESC 71 , [2018] 1 I.R. 375 in which Clarke CJ observed: 

 "67. The requirement that the court be "local" clearly causes no difficulties in cases such as this for the property jurisdiction of the Circuit Court is ordinarily conferred on the circuit in which the property concerned is situated. The issue which arose for debate was, however concerned with the requirement that the jurisdiction be "limited". On that basis it was said that the court might be required, in order that the interpretation to be placed on the legislation was consistent with the Constitution, to refrain from adopting an interpretation which would confer an unlimited jurisdiction on the Circuit Court in cases such as this." 

 He went on to say: 

 " 74. A real meaning must be given to the requirement that the jurisdiction of a court such as the Circuit Court is limited. To do otherwise would be to disregard the Constitution. But it is not necessary to go so far as to require that each and every category of case in which a jurisdiction is conferred on the Circuit Court must have a monetary or value limitation. However, that being said, it might be the case that to confer a jurisdiction in a very wide category of case without any limitation might cause constitutional difficulties." 

 The observations of Clarke C.J. in that case focussed principally on the nature of the "limited" jurisdiction of the Circuit Court but while that was the principal issue, his observations on the "local" jurisdiction are of importance. As he noted in that case, jurisdiction is " ordinarily conferred on the circuit in which the property concerned is situated". Just as it is the case that the jurisdiction of the Circuit Court is ordinarily restricted in property disputes to the area in which the property is situated, there are also limitations on where proceedings can be brought in family law proceedings. In this context, Order 59 of the Rules of the Circuit Court provides for the venue for such proceedings, in the county where the applicant or a child to whom the application relates ordinarily resides. There is also provision for proceedings to be brought where the applicant carries on any profession, business or occupation. Thus, the Circuit Court is not at large in terms of the location in which it exercises its jurisdiction. I am conscious of the fact that a party commencing proceedings in the Circuit Court may, on the facts of a particular case, have a choice of venue. It could, for example, be where the other party resides or works. In some cases the choice of venue may be restricted, for example, in proceedings relating to property. This view applies also to the jurisdiction of the District Court. It is limited as to venue in making orders by reference to the relevant District Court's particular functional area. Thus, it follows that  an order made by the Circuit Court could not be enforced other than in a Circuit in which the particular Circuit is the appropriate venue for any necessary proceedings, as determined by the Rules of the Circuit Court. It is important not to overstate the geographical limitations on the jurisdictions of the Circuit and District Courts. An order of each of those Courts is of validity regardless of where it has been made but it's enforceability by courts in other Circuits or Districts is limited by reference to the Rules of those Courts as to venue. For example, a judgment of the Dublin Circuit Court for damages in a personal injuries action is not a judgment which is valid only in Dublin. It can be enforced elsewhere in the country, provided that the place in which it is sought to enforced is a place which has jurisdiction to enforce it, because, for example,  the judgment debtor has property there. Thus, an Isaac Wunder order, whether made by the District Court or the Circuit Court is of validity throughout the country as a whole and restricts the person bound by such an order from issuing fresh proceedings elsewhere in the country. I appreciate the fact that Collins J. in a judgment which he is about to deliver herein takes a different view on this question (see para 18 et seq. thereof) but for my part, I do not take the view that the essence of the local and limited jurisdiction of the Circuit Court or, indeed, the District Court, is such that an order made in one Circuit or District cannot have legal effect outside the boundaries of that Circuit or District. It is important to bear in  mind that an Isaac Wunder  order made against an individual litigant in respect of litigation involving the same party in respect of the same type of litigation is effective regardless of the Circuit or District in which it was made. However, it is important to remember the limits of the jurisdiction of those courts. A party can only initiate proceedings in a venue which has jurisdiction to deal with the matter, Thus, an  Isaac Wunder order will only be effective in a Circuit or District in which the relevant Court would otherwise have jurisdiction to deal with the matter.  This is because the nature of such an order is that it is an order in personam  and is limited to the parties in the relevant litigation. An Isaac Wunder order should reflect these limitations and should not be formulated by the Circuit or District Court in such a way as to preclude the party the subject of the order from litigating against other parties not involved in the subject litigation or in respect of other issues which are unrelated to the subject matter of the litigation affected by the order. That is not to suggest that the High Court in the exercise of its full and original jurisdiction cannot make more extensive orders where appropriate. Accordingly, I agree with the views expressed by Murray J. in the judgment he is about to deliver on this issue. For completeness, I should add that I agree with the views of Hogan J. on this issue as set out in his judgment herein. 

 156.           Finally, reference should also be made to Grimes v Owners of SS Bangor Bay [1948] I.R. 350, an admiralty action, in which O'Byrne J. considered Article 34.3.4° by referring back to Article 64 of the Constitution of 1922, part of which was in similar terms, saying at p. 358: 

 "that it enjoine[d] and require[d] that [the Circuit Court] should be local and limited in its jurisdiction.. [Though one Court] its jurisdiction is to be exercised locally by the judges of that court in the manner specified by s.52 and this section was intended, in my opinion, to satisfy the constitutional requirement that the jurisdiction of courts of first instance, other than the High Court, should be local...If a statute purported to confer upon any court of first instance, other than the High Court, such unlimited jurisdiction, it would, in my opinion, contravene the clear intendment of the Constitution." 

 157.              While there may be possibly be a difference in emphasis between what was said by O'Byrne J. in Grimes and the subsequent comments of Clarke C.J. in Langan, the key point which emerges from both decisions is that the local and limited requirement simply requires that the jurisdiction of the District Court and the Circuit Court must be rooted by reference to venue. The interpretation of this is, however, largely a matter for the Oireachtas: Article 34.3.4⁰ is largely accommodating in nature rather than being prescriptive in character. While neither the District Court or the Circuit Court can be invested with what amounts to the High Court's full original jurisdiction, then in Casey's words ("The Constitution and the Legal System" (1979) 14 Irish Jurist 1 at 14): 

 "Short of this, the extent and amplitude of jurisdiction conferred on the lower courts would seem to be a matter within the discretion of the Oireachtas. The Constitution, as the framework for government in a changing society, must surely be interpreted to afford the flexibility which social and economic developments may require. Restrictions on the jurisdiction of the Circuit Court thought appropriate twenty years ago may no longer be suitable; and in so far as they depend on the absence of appropriate machinery in that court, the remedy is plainly in the hands of Government and the Oireachtas." 

 I consider that this passage neatly summarises the effect of the local and limited requirements contained in Article 34.3.4.⁰ 

 158.              Finally, as observed previously, I am satisfied that the Circuit Court cannot make an order restricting the issue of proceedings in the High Court. Equally, I cannot see any basis for the District Court to make any order restricting the issue of proceedings in the Circuit Court. It must be borne in mind that the power of the courts to make these types of orders is to protect such courts from an abuse of process before the relevant court. I am fortified in this view by the express words of  s. 22 (6) of the 1961 Act set out above which provides that the Circuit  Court has jurisdiction "as regards any cause of action for the time being within its jurisdiction " (my emphasis). 

 159.              Given the clear limits on the exercise of such power, it follows that the limited jurisdiction of both the District Court and the Circuit Court could not be such as to enable such Courts to make orders restricting the issue of proceedings in Courts which enjoy a greater jurisdiction under the Constitution. 

 

 The Court of Appeal Order: Discussion 

 160.              A number of points were made by the appellant in arguing that the Court of Appeal erred in making an Isaac Wunder order in this case. First of all, reference was made to the fact that less intrusive measures were not considered which might have the same effect as an Isaac Wunde r order, while respecting the appellant's rights and the best interests of the child. It was submitted that the making of an Isaac Wunder order did not accord with the principle of proportionality. It was also said that the Court of Appeal failed to have regard to the best interests of the child. Further, it was argued that the Court of Appeal failed to have regard to the dynamic nature of family law disputes. It was then suggested that the Court of Appeal should have considered making an order that was time-limited, or specific issue-related, rather than a blanket prohibition on issuing proceedings or applications. In these circumstances, it was said that the Isaac Wunder order made herein was disproportionate and unduly restrictive. 

 161.              For her part, the respondent took issue with the contention that the making of an Isaac Wunder order was disproportionate. She pointed out that such orders are only made in exceptional cases, upon proof of the type of exceptional circumstances that are required to enable the making of such order. She takes issue with the arguments that there was any error on the part of the Court of Appeal in making that order. She made the point that the Court of Appeal in this case would have been in error had it not made an Isaac Wunder order, and went on to point out that a failure to make such an order in a case of this kind would have the effect of depriving the respondent of an important remedy, in circumstances where she had been subjected to unduly protracted, oppressive, vexatious, and unnecessarily costly family litigation. 

 162.              In order to consider this issue properly, it is necessary to look at the judgment of the Court of Appeal of the 28 th June, 2024, in which it opted to make an Isaac Wunder order. In that regard, the Court of Appeal had regard to the decision in the case of Riordan v. Ireland (No. 4) , the case of M.M. v. G.M. , S.P. v. U.G. , all referred to above previously, and, finally, Burke v. Judge Fulham [2010] IEHC 448 . Woulfe J. set out the principles identified by Irvine J. (as she then was) in the Burke case, set out at para. 12 above. 

 163.              Having observed that he agreed with the approach set out by Irvine J. in Burke , Woulfe J. added that: 

 "... the above factors should be looked at in a broad untechnical way, as a list of potential factors capable of adaptation and extension, rather than in any literal or mechanical way, having regard to the broad nature of the jurisdiction described by this Court in Riordan (No. 4)." 

 164.              He then applied the legal principles set out in Burke to the facts of this case (see paras. 13 - 15 above). While the appellant complained that the Court of Appeal in its judgment did not have regard to the best interests of the child, I think this is, to some extent, a mischaracterisation of the way in which the Court of Appeal dealt with the matter. The Court of Appeal had regard to three uncontested affidavits sworn by the respondent herein setting out the actions of the appellant. The Court clearly had regard to all of the facts and circumstances in the case. That included the fact that the nature of the litigation was causing " significant stress and anxiety on the part of the minor child " (judgment, para. 8). 

 165.              For my part, I am satisfied that the Court of Appeal did not err in making the Isaac Wunder order, having regard to the facts and circumstances of this case. The respondent herein has been subjected to a barrage of unmeritorious litigation. As Woulfe J. said at para. 30: 

 "... a situation has been reached where to permit the [appellant] an unrestricted right to continue to litigate against the respondent would be unfair and oppressive to the respondent, and a waste of scarce court time and resources to the detriment of other litigants." 

 166.              This litigation has occurred at a great cost to the respondent, both in terms of stress and anxiety and in financial terms. Restricting such litigation by way of an Isaac Wunder is an entirely appropriate response to the behaviour of the appellant. 

 167.              While the appellant urged this Court to adopt a less restrictive approach in the circumstances of this type of litigation in particular, involving a family dispute, I see no merit in that suggestion. While an Isaac Wunder order restricts a litigant from issuing new proceedings or applications, it is a restriction which can be lifted by prior leave of the President of the court concerned. In a case in which it is appropriate to grant leave, that will be done. There is no reason why any application for leave could not be dealt with expeditiously. Accordingly, there is no basis for overturning the decision of the Court of Appeal in this regard. 

 General Powers of  the Court when presented with Serial Litigants: Discussion 

 168.              The appellant in dealing with this issue referred to the fact that the courts have a range of powers at their disposal to safeguard the administration of justice. However, it was reiterated that any restriction on the right of access to the courts had to be proportionate, respect the principle of legal certainty, and uphold a litigant's fundamental rights under both the Constitution and the Convention. 

 169.              It was argued that the principle of proportionality requires that any restriction imposed is the least restrictive measure necessary to achieve the legitimate aim of preventing abuse. Reference was made to the decision in Brumarescu v. Romania (App. No. 28342/95) [1999] VII E.H.R.R. 862, in which the European Court of Human Rights, referring to Article 6.1 of the Convention, pointed out that: 

 "One of the fundamental aspects of the rule of law is the principle of legal certainty, ..." 

 170.              It was suggested on behalf of the appellant that the current approach to the making of Isaac Wunder orders does not fully accord with the principle of legal certainty and, once more, the appellant urged on this Court that a model such as that employed in the courts of England and Wales, referred to above, was a more structured and transparent framework within which to deal with vexatious litigants. Accordingly, it was submitted that a more calibrated approach to restraining orders should be adopted in this jurisdiction. 

 171.              For her part, the respondent referred to a number of powers of the courts, such as the power to strike out or dismiss proceedings, the power in relation to the making of costs orders or requiring security for costs, the use of case management to discourage delay, and the jurisdiction of the courts in relation to contempt. Reference was also made to the power of a court to strike out proceedings under O. 19, r. 28 of the RSC. It was pointed out that, in circumstances where it was necessary to clarify or correct a misrepresentation about prior proceedings, a transcript of the proceedings could be obtained, and that would include, in appropriate cases, the digital audio recording of previous proceedings. However, the point was made that none of the remedies available in ordinary civil litigation could address misconduct in the context of family law litigation, because of the fact that principles such as res judicata , issue estoppel, and the rule in Henderson v. Henderson (1843) 3 Hare 100 , 67 ER 313 were not readily applicable to some issues in family law proceedings. As I pointed out previously, certain family law orders cannot be regarded as 'final' in the way that a final order is understood in relation to ordinary civil litigation. In that context, the respondent submitted an Isaac Wunder order was an appropriate remedy in such proceedings. 

 172.              She made the point that such orders can be obtained in a manner which is inherently flexible and efficient. She submitted that, as an application for leave to bring proceedings or a further application is made before the President or nominated judge who must deal with the matter constitutionally by reference to the rights of all affected parties, having regard to both the Constitution and the Convention, that it was a fluid and fair process which admits of a variety of orders shaped to the nature of the case. She argued that the absence of statutory rules in this country heightened the need to maintain the availability of Isaac Wunder orders, as it is a necessary tool to protect the courts processes and to prevent abuse by vexatious litigants. The fact that a party against whom such an order is made retains the right to obtain leave or, indeed, in an appropriate case, to apply to have the Isaac Wunder order vacated upon the showing of good reason, requires courts to adhere to the principles of justice and to balance the rights of all affected parties in a proportionate manner. 

 173.              The Attorney General in his submissions likewise referred to a number of the inherent powers of the courts, such as: 

 ·          the power to strike out proceedings as an abuse of process, or otherwise doomed to fail; 

 ·          the dismissal of proceedings where the litigant's conduct makes their continuation impossible; 

 ·          the making of an order restraining a litigant from bringing proceedings without permission against a named party, or in particular proceedings; 

 ·          the making of an order restraining a litigant from bringing proceedings without permission that relate to, or touch on, an issue previously determined in other proceedings; 

 ·          the making of an order restraining a litigant from bringing proceedings without permission in general; 

 ·          the making of orders in any of the above requiring that a litigant seek permission in writing only, and/or specified judge(s); 

 ·          the making of an order requiring that a litigant provide security for costs prior to the bringing of proceedings in any of the above situations; 

 ·          the making of an order for costs in any of the above situations that measures costs and requires that they be discharged prior to any further application being brought; 

 ·          the making of orders freezing or otherwise sequestering assets where they may be used to prevent default of the court orders above; 

 ·          the use of the contempt jurisdiction to protect the process or integrity of the court process; 

 ·          the imposition of an injunction preventing a litigant from being present in the precincts of a court building without permission; 

 ·          the imposition of an injunction preventing a litigant from seeking to address a court on their own behalf, and/or as a McKenzie friend. 

 174.              As was pointed out on behalf of the Attorney General, such powers would require to be balanced against competing considerations, including the constitutional right of access to the courts. It was acknowledged that this was an aspect of the  rights protected by Article 6 of the Convention. As was noted, the right of access to the courts is not an absolute right and may be subject to appropriate limitations. The observations of Noonan J. in the case of Leslie Fitzsimons v. Bank of Scotland Plc. & Tanager Ltd. [2019] IECA 336 were referred to, in which it was stated at para. 24 as follows: 

 "The making of an Isaac Wunder order is not an abrogation of the constitutional right of access to the court, but rather a proportionate filtering mechanism to protect the opposing party from the injustice of having to incur what are often very significant and unrecoverable costs, in meeting oppressive and abusive claims." 

 175.              Reference was also made in the submissions of the Attorney General to the case of Kearney v. Bank of Scotland Plc. [2020] IECA 92 . At para. 132, the Court of Appeal in its judgment set out a number of principles to be applied to the making of Isaac Wunder orders. It said: 

 "Isaac Wunder orders now form part of the panoply of the courts' inherent powers to regulate their own process. In light of the constitutional protection of the right of access to the courts, such orders should be deployed sparingly and only be made where a clear case has been made out that demonstrates the necessity of the making of the orders in the circumstances: 

 i.        Regard can be had by the court to the history of litigation between the parties or other parties connected with them in relation to common issues. 

 ii.       Regard can be had also to the nature of allegations advanced and in particular where scurrilous or outrageous statements are asserted including fraud against a party to litigation or their legal representatives or other professionals connected with the other party to the litigation. 

 iii.      The court ought to be satisfied that there are good grounds for believing that there will be further proceedings instituted by a claimant before an Isaac Wunder type order restraining the prosecution of litigation or the institution of fresh litigation is made. 

 iv.      Regard may be had to the issue of costs and the conduct of the litigant in question with regard to the payment and discharge of costs orders incurred up to the date of the making of the order by defendants and indeed by past defendants in applications connected with the issues the subject matter of the litigation. 

 v.       The balancing exercise between the competing rights of the parties is to be carried out with due regard to the constitutional rights of a litigant and in general no legitimate claim brought by a plaintiff ought to be precluded from being heard and determined in a court of competent jurisdiction save in exceptional circumstances. 

 vi.      It is not the function of the courts to protect a litigant from his own insatiable appetite for litigation and an Isaac Wunder type order is intended to operate preferably as an early stage compulsory filter, necessitated by the interests of the common good and the need to ensure that limited court resources are available to those who require same most and not dissipated and for the purposes of saving money and time for all parties and for the court. 

 vii.     Such orders should provide a delimitation on access to the court only to the extent necessitated in the interests of the common good. 

 viii.     Regard should be had to the fact that the right of access to the courts to determine a genuine and serious dispute about the existence of a right or interest, subject to limitations clearly defined in the jurisprudence and by statute, is constitutionally protected, was enshrined in clause 40 of Magna Carta of 1215 and is incorporated into the European Convention on Human Rights by article 6, to which the courts have regard in the administration of justice in this jurisdiction since the coming into operation of the European Convention on Human Rights Act 2003. 

 ix.      The courts should be vigilant in regard to making such orders in circumstances where a litigant is unrepresented and may not be in a position to properly articulate his interests in maintaining access to the courts. Where possible the litigant ought to be forewarned of an intended application for an Isaac Wunder type order. In the instant case it is noteworthy that the trial judge afforded the appellant the option of giving an undertaking to refrain from taking further proceedings which he declined. 

 x.       Any power which a court may have to prevent, restrain or delimit a party from commencing or pursuing legal proceedings must be regarded as exceptional. It appears that inferior courts do not have such inherent power to prevent a party from initiating or pursuing proceedings at any level. 

 xi.      An Isaac Wunder order may have serious implications for the party against whom it is made. It potentially stigmatises such a litigant by branding her or him as, in effect, "vexatious" and this may present a risk of inherent bias in the event that a fresh application is made for leave to institute proceedings in respect of the subject matter of the order or to set aside a stay granted in litigation. 

 xii.     Where a strike out order can be made or an order dismissing litigation whether as an abuse of process or pursuant to the inherent jurisdiction of the court or pursuant to the provisions of O. 19, r. 28, same is to be preferred and a clear and compelling case must be identified as to why, in addition, an Isaac Wunder type order is necessitated by the party seeking it." 

 176.              Much of what is stated in that passage requires little or no elaboration, and reflects some important considerations; firstly, the fact that the making of an Isaac Wunder order should be a last resort and is not an order which should be lightly or routinely made. Secondly, the possibility of other alternatives that might be available and meet the purpose of bringing vexatious litigation to an end could be considered. A key factor in any case is the fact that the making of an Isaac Wunder order does, in fact, restrict a person's right of access to the courts, and thus this is an important consideration for any court contemplating the making of such order, albeit, as explained above, it is a restriction which, at most, interposes an additional procedural step before the issuing of fresh proceedings, where leave will be granted in an appropriate case. 

 177.              The Attorney General went on in his submissions to say that the powers of the Court to deal with such matters, and litigation that can be described as vexatious or an abuse of process, are " inherently flexible and capable of being adapted and applied so that any order made reflects the requirements of balance and proportionality in a particular case ". That is undoubtedly the case. The Attorney General went on to make the point that the principles referred to in Kearney should not be regarded as a form of checklist, each step of which have to be complied with before an order could be made. Again, I would agree with that submission. The one point I would make is that, for reasons already explained, I do not agree with the observation at point (x) to the effect that " it appears that inferior courts do not have any such inherent power to prevent a party from initiating or pursuing proceedings at any level " save that as noted previously, I agree with Simons J.'s observation in relation to the extent of the power of the Circuit Court in this case, and that it could not make an order that would oust the jurisdiction of the High Court (see para. 16 of his judgment referred to previously herein) and is limited to making such orders within its own jurisdiction as explained above. 

 178.              Thus, in relation to the question posed by the Court in this regard, as to the powers that a court may generally exercise when presented with a serial litigant, there is no doubt but that there are a wide number of remedies available to a court to deal with such litigants. In the case of Isaac Wunder orders, it is important to remember that the making of such an order does no more than restrict a party from access to the courts without prior leave to the President of the court, or a judge nominated by the President of that court. It is not a blanket ban on somebody issuing proceedings, for example, for a period of two years. It is simply the requirement of a party to make an application for leave before embarking on fresh proceedings. Yes, it does restrict the right of access to court, but, as has been explained, it is a form of order that is the last resort in cases where parties are the subject of oppressive litigation. It is important to observe that orders such as this are not made every day by courts in this country. The circumstances in which such orders could be made will only arise in limited circumstances. The effect of not making such orders where appropriate is to cause further distress, anxiety, and oppression to parties affected by such litigation. It is also fair to say that cases of the kind in which such orders have to be made frequently involve the excessive use of court time which, as has been emphasised previously, is scarce. Thus, two interests are served by the making of such orders, namely, the interests of the individuals affected by the making of such an order, but also the requirements of the courts to ensure that their time is not unduly spent on hopeless, vexatious, and pointless litigation. 

 179.              There is one further point to note. When a court is satisfied that it is appropriate, having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case, to make an Isaac Wunder order, it should be borne in mind that the party against whom the order has been made will, in general, have a right of appeal. As was pointed out by the Attorney General in response to questions raised by the Court, an appeal against a decision of a lower court which made an Isaac Wunder order, or an appeal against a refusal of a lower court to grant leave to bring proceedings, may involve the other party to those proceedings in further litigation concerning the appeal. Restrictions on a right to appeal are problematic. In the case of Governey v. Financial Services Ombudsman [2015] IESC 38 , [2015] 2 I.R. 616, Clarke J. addressed the issue of restrictions on the right of appeal and said at pp. 623 to 624 as follows: 

 " The point which I wish to emphasise is not that there is anything inappropriate about legislation restricting or, in appropriate cases, excluding a right of appeal. Rather, the point is that where such restriction or exclusion is sought to be achieved, it should be done by clear wording ." 

 180.              Two provisions govern appeals from the District Court to the Circuit Court, and from the Circuit Court to the High Court. Thus, s. 84 of the Courts of Justice Act 1924 provides that an appeal shall lie " in all cases other than criminal cases " from any decision of the District Court to the Circuit Court. 

 181.              So far as the Circuit Court is concerned, provision is made in ss. 37 and 38 of the Courts of Justice Act 1936, providing for an appeal to the High Court from the judgment or order in any civil action or matter. The legislation clearly does not affect the right of appeal in the case of Isaac Wunder orders. Accordingly, it is the view of the Attorney General that any order made restricting a party by way of an Isaac Wunder order, or indeed refusing leave to bring further proceedings, must be appealable. I am satisfied that this is so. It follows that the making of an Isaac Wunder order is, by its very nature, an exceptional order, and will only be made when it is necessary and proportionate to do so. The making of any such order will usually be appealable (provided it is made by a court from which an appeal lies), and, finally, insofar as it is a restriction on the right of access to justice, it is subject to the possibility of leave being granted to permit further proceedings to be issued, if appropriate to grant such leave. 

 182.              One other issue was raised in this context, and it is in relation to a situation where somebody has misrepresented what occurred in court on a previous occasion. It will be recalled that these proceedings commenced by way of proceedings for judicial review on foot of an ex parte application for leave to apply for judicial review which came before Simons J. in the first instance in August 2022. Subsequently, the respondent issued a motion seeking to set aside the grant of leave. She set out the background to the matter and raised serious issues as to the information provided to the High Court on the application for judicial review. Simons J. considered the principles applicable to setting aside a grant of leave, and noted that, in circumstances of material non-disclosure on the part of an applicant, it was possible to make an order setting aside the grant of leave. In this regard, it would be helpful to refer to para. 23 of the judgment of the Court of Appeal of the 28 th February, 2024 ( [2024] IECA 45 ) , in which the following was recorded: 

 "23.     The trial judge turned next to applying these principles to the circumstances of the present case. It was apparent to him that the applicant's characterisation of the Circuit Court hearing on the 23rd May, 2022, was grossly misleading. First, it was simply untrue to say that there was no evidence before the Circuit Court in relation to the outstanding maintenance payments, in circumstances where the respondent had given sworn oral evidence to the Court on that date and specifically confirmed that there was a sum of 3,265 outstanding. Secondly, the averment that counsel for the applicant had sought to cross examine the respondent was also untrue. Thirdly, the applicant's averment that no supportive affidavit had been sworn by the respondent was incorrect as the respondent had, in fact, filed three affidavits in support of her appeal from the District Court. 

 24.       More generally, Simons J. held that the applicant had failed to disclose the convoluted history of these family law proceedings, the case having been listed for hearing before the Circuit Court on more than forty occasions, with multiple interim orders having been made. The false impression created by the applicant's verifying affidavit was that the appeal had been determined in a peremptory manner by the Circuit Court." 

 183.              As was noted by the Court of Appeal, the trial judge found that the description of the hearing before the Circuit Court, as per the statement of grounds and verifying affidavit, was grossly misleading and conveyed the false impression that the Court had acted in breach of fair procedures and the basic rules of evidence. 

 184.              The Court of Appeal went on to conclude that, with the exception in relation to the part of the case relating to the making of the Isaac Wunder order, the trial judge was justified in setting aside almost all of the grant of leave. As the Court of Appeal said " the applicant's misstatements and non-disclosure were of a serious nature, and must be deprecated by this Court ...". 

 185.              One of the questions that falls for consideration is the nature of the powers of a court when a party before it misrepresents what occurred in court on a previous occasion. In this case, the issue arose in the context of an application for judicial review. Such proceedings are initiated generally by way of ex parte application. As such, there is an obligation of utmost good faith on the part of the person initiating the application. If that requirement is not adhered to, in an appropriate case, a respondent can make an application to have the grant of leave set aside. In this case, that was done in accordance with well-established case law. 

 186.              As was noted in the Court of Appeal, the basis upon which leave was granted fell away when it became clear that there had been no denial of fair procedures by the judge in the Circuit Court when hearing the matter originally. As such, the basis for judicial review had not been met. Central to the making of the application to set aside was the affidavit of the respondent who was able to aver to the fact that what was stated by the appellant in his grounding affidavit was simply not correct and was, in fact, misleading. Thus, the High Court and the Court of Appeal were in a position to confirm that the application for judicial review should be set aside subject to the limitation in relation to the Isaac Wunder order. It is of note that, in dealing with this matter, the High Court had the benefit of a transcript of the hearing before the Circuit Court. Although it is not stated to be the case, I presume that the transcript of the Circuit Court hearing was obtained by reference to the digital audio recording (DAR) when the application for leave to apply for judicial review was made (see para. 6 of the judgment of Simons J.). It would be unusual for the parties to have arranged for a stenographer to record the evidence in Circuit Court family law proceedings and, therefore it is likely that this was done by the production of the DAR. 

 187.              As stated above, the courts have the power to set aside an application for leave to apply for judicial review brought on a basis which is factually misleading, or as it was in this case, " grossly misleading ". That in itself is sufficient to deal with a situation such as that which occurred in this case. It is also important to note that, as a matter of practice, digital audio recording takes place in virtually every court throughout the country. It is an important safeguard for the parties before the court and, more importantly, for the courts themselves, to ensure that what occurs in court is not subsequently misrepresented. One would hope that it is not necessary on a regular basis to be required to have recourse to the DAR to actually ascertain what occurred in a particular court in the face of allegations as to what was said to have happened, or not, as the case may be. In any event, the availability of the DAR is an important safeguard to ensure the integrity of court proceedings. Accordingly, in a case where allegations of the kind that occurred in this case arise, there will be some sense of security in knowing that there is available, if needed, a record of what transpired in court. That is the most fundamental protection in relation to parties who misrepresent what occurred in court. 

 Application for leave to bring further proceedings notwithstanding the making of an Isaac Wunder order 

 188.              As was noted in the submissions of the Attorney General, the decision in Riordan v. Ireland (No. 5) [2001] 4 I.R. 463 sets out the basis upon which an application for leave to issue further proceedings can be made. In that case, Ó Caoimh J. set out the test for obtaining leave (p. 465): 

 "Where the court is satisfied that a person has habitually or persistently instituted vexatious or frivolous civil proceedings it may make an order restraining the institution of further proceedings against parties to those earlier proceedings without prior leave of the court. In assessment of the question whether the proceedings are vexatious the court is entitled to look at the whole history of the matter and it is not confined to a consideration as to whether the pleadings disclose a cause of action. The court is entitled in the assessment of whether proceedings are vexatious to consider whether they have been brought without any reasonable ground. The court has to determine whether the proceedings being brought are being brought without any reasonable ground or have been brought habitually and persistently without reasonable ground." 

 189.              In the course of that case, Ó Caoimh J. referred to a Canadian case Re Lang Michener and Fabian (1987) 37 D.L.R. (4th) 685 at p. 691, in which the following matters were set out as tending to show that a proceeding is vexatious: 

 "(a)     the bringing up on one or more actions to determine an issue which has already been determined by a court of competent jurisdiction; 

 (b)       where it is obvious that an action cannot succeed, or if the action would lead to no possible good, or if no reasonable person can reasonably expect to obtain relief; 

 (c)        where the action is brought for an improper purpose, including the harassment and oppression of other parties by multifarious proceedings brought for purposes other than the assertion of legitimate rights; 

 (d)       where issues tend to be rolled forward into subsequent actions and repeated and supplemented, often with actions brought against the lawyers who have acted for or against the litigant in earlier proceedings; 

 (e)        where the person instituting the proceedings has failed to pay the cost of unsuccessful proceedings; 

 (f)        where the respondent persistently takes unsuccessful appeals from judicial decisions." 

 190.              The comment was made by Cooke J. in the case of Kenny v. An Bord Pleanála [2010] IEHC 321 , to the effect that a court ought not to grant leave by way of exception to an Isaac Wunder order: 

 "... unless it is satisfied that the claim proposed to be served is not a vexatious repetition of the same grievance already disposed of and that it is not a claim which is manifestly unfounded or unstateable." 

 191.              Similar views were expressed by Peart J. in Daire v. The Wise Finance Company Ltd. [2018] IECA 126 at para. 18. Accordingly, it was submitted on behalf of the Attorney General that a court granting leave to bring proceedings should be satisfied: 

 1.       That the legal claim being advanced is not a repetition of previous claims or grievances on the part of the applicant, which claims have been the subject of final determination(s) by the courts; 

 2.       The legal claim being advanced is an arguable one which the applicant has a demonstrable interest in litigating. 

 192.              For his part, the appellant also referred to the decision in Riordan (No. 5) , and emphasised the fact that the test to be applied is an objective test and must balance the right of access to the courts with the need to prevent abuse of the judicial process. I have no difficulty with that contention. The respondent made the point that, when determining whether or not to grant leave, the court will necessarily consider the reasons being offered for the further litigation by reference to the previous proceedings brought by the applicant and the context in which the Isaac Wunder order was granted in the case. Where arguable grounds are shown in a bona fide manner by such an applicant, then the jurisprudence outlined above requires the court to grant the requested leave. Equally, that seems to me to be uncontroversial. 

 193.              It is abundantly clear that, in considering any such application, a court will, of necessity, have to consider the history of the previous litigation between the applicant requesting leave and the person or persons in whose favour the Isaac Wunder order was made. If legitimate grounds for bringing proceedings are established then, provided that there is an arguable claim to be brought and the applicant for leave has a proper interest in litigating the issue, leave should be granted. For my part, I am satisfied that the test for leave as articulated in the cases referred to above does not need to be adjusted.  It is important to emphasise that on any such application for leave, it will be important to have regard to the proceedings which have already taken place and the reasons why an Isaac Wunder order was granted in the first place.  

 Conclusions 

 194.              An Isaac Wunder order is one of the many inherent powers of the courts which can be employed, in exceptional circumstances, to prevent abuse of the judicial process. In light of the constitutional protection of the right of access to the courts, such orders are not an absolute bar to litigation, but operate as a filtering mechanism to restrain the repeated initiation of vexatious or unmeritorious proceedings. As the authorities make clear, an Isaac Wunder order will only be made where it is considered proportionate and necessary to do so, and the safeguard of a right of appeal will generally be available to the affected party. Such orders are not confined to the jurisdiction of the superior courts but may be made by the Circuit and District Courts in the exercise of their inherent powers to prevent an abuse of process in their courts within their jurisdiction. 

 195.              With regard to the specific context of family law proceedings, I find that there is nothing to prevent the making of an Isaac Wunder order in proceedings concerning child access, custody, or maintenance disputes. The best interests of a child is a relevant factor to consider before making such an order. As is demonstrated by the present appeal, however, a child's best interests may well be adversely affected by repetitious litigation and the consequent familial and financial strain caused by such proceedings. In this respect, I am satisfied that the Isaac Wunder order made by the Court of Appeal was neither disproportionate nor unduly restrictive, but rather a necessary response to a campaign of unmeritorious and oppressive litigation on the part of appellant on the basis of the evidence before the Court. 

 196.              Finally, it has been observed that, in addition to the power to issue an Isaac Wunder order, the courts have a range of powers at their disposal to safeguard the administration of justice when presented with a serial litigant or someone who disrupts or prolongs proceedings on a repeated basis as set out above. Where an application for leave to apply for judicial review is brought on a basis which is factually misleading, an application to set aside the grant of leave may be appropriate, as it was in the present case. Further, the availability of the DAR is an important safeguard to ensure the integrity of court proceedings where parties misrepresent what occurred in court on a previous occasion. These powers and procedures help to ensure that the twin objectives of protecting individual parties from serial or vexatious litigation and protecting the judicial process from excessive misuse of court time and resources, are realised. 

 197.              Accordingly, I would dismiss the appeal and affirm the order of the Court of Appeal.

 AN CHÚIRT UACHTARACH 

 THE SUPREME COURT 

 S:AP:IE:2024:000124 

 Dunne J. 

 Charleton J. 

 Hogan J. 

 Murray J. 

 Collins J. 


 [2026] IESC 2 

 BETWEEN/ 

 GM 

 APPLICANT/APPELLANT 

 AND 

   

 IM 

 RESPONDENT 

 AND 

 THE ATTORNEY GENERAL 

 NOTICE PARTY 

 JUDGMENT of Mr. Justice Gerard Hogan delivered on the 23 rd day of  January 2026 

 

 1.       This appeal presents two important issues. First, do the Circuit Court and the District Court each have a jurisdiction to grant an Isaac Wunder order to prevent abusive litigation by a particular litigant? Second, if so, do the Circuit Court and the District Court each have a jurisdiction to grant an Isaac Wunder order which takes effect throughout the State and outside of the territorial limits of that court's jurisdiction? As the facts and the relevant legal issues have been comprehensively set out in the judgment of Dunne J., I can proceed immediately to address these issues. 

 The jurisdiction of the Circuit Court and the District Court to grant an Isaac Wunder order 

 2.        I entirely agree with the judgment which Dunne J. has just delivered to the effect that the Circuit Court and the District Court each enjoy such a jurisdiction in principle to grant Isaac Wunder orders. Article 34.1 of the Constitution vests the administration of justice in the judicial branch of government. As I pointed out in Kirwan v. Connors [2025] IESC 21 , this constitutional provision essentially designates the judiciary as the custodians of the administration of justice so that each court is obliged to ensure not only that the judicial process works efficiently and fairly, but also that this process is not used for oblique or abusive purposes. To that extent, it may be regarded as a regulation of the constitutional right of access to the courts which is also protected by Article 34.1 (read, if necessary, in conjunction with Article 40.3): see, for example, Murphy v. Greene [1990] 2 IR 566 at 578, where McCarthy J. referred to the Isaac Wunder jurisdiction in these terms. 

 3.       The making of an Isaac Wunder order accordingly serves the constitutional purposes which were identified in Kirwan v. Connors by ensuring that an abusive litigant cannot harass or oppress his opponent by repeated, fruitless litigation. While it may have been true a generation ago to say, as Costello J. did in O'Malley v. Irish Nationwide Building Society , High Court, 21st January 1984, that such an order would be made only "in very rare circumstances", this is, I think, no longer quite the case. These words were uttered in what were, perhaps, simpler times for the legal system. They came at a time when McCarthy J. could offer the view that it was doubtful "if the court records reveal many or even any instances of such officious interference" by abusive litigants: see Norris v. Attorney General [1984] IR 36 at 91. For whatever reason, oppressive litigation has, regrettably, become far more common since the mid-1980s. 

 4.       One way or another, therefore, I agree that the development of the Isaac Wunder jurisdiction is a necessary and indispensable feature of the administration of justice so that these constitutionally derived powers must be deemed to be vested in both the Circuit Court and the District Court. I also agree with Collins J. that it would be desirable that the parameters of this jurisdiction were regulated by law. While it might be useful if this jurisdiction was regulated by statute law, it should, at a minimum, also be regulated by Rules of Court. 

 The local and limited jurisdiction of the Circuit Court and the District Court 

 5.       I now turn to the more difficult question in this appeal: can the Circuit Court or the District Court make an Isaac Wunder order with nationwide effect? (This is not an issue in the case of the High Court given that it enjoys a full original jurisdiction by virtue of Article 34.3.1⁰.) It is true that this Court has frequently observed in cases such as Grimes v. Owners of SS Bangor Bay [1948] IR 350 and The State (Boyle) v. Neylon [1986] IR 551 that the Circuit Court is one Court. It is nonetheless, like the District Court, also a court of local and limited jurisdiction for the purposes of Article 34.3.4⁰. While the courts have sometimes struggled to ascribe a fixed and consistent meaning to these constitutional requirements, nonetheless as Clarke C.J. observed in Permanent TSB plc v. Langan [2017] IESC 71 , [2018] 1 IR 375 at 397, a "real meaning must be given to the requirement that the jurisdiction of a court such as the Circuit Court is limited." 

 6.       In the context of the "local" requirement, this means that the jurisdiction of the Circuit Court must be bounded in some way by geographical considerations.  This does not mean that the hands of the Oireachtas are tied by reference to the considerations which governed the allocation of jurisdiction to the Circuit Court and District Court in 1937 or even in 1961 at the time of the enactment of the Courts (Supplemental Provisions) Act 1961. The Oireachtas is, in principle, free to experiment in respect of the allocation of jurisdiction to the District and Circuit Courts. After all, Article 36.iii envisages that - subject, of course, to the requirements of Article 34 itself from which it may not derogate - the Oireachtas will legislate to regulate "the distribution of jurisdiction and business" of the courts. 

 7.       What it does mean, however, is that the Oireachtas must nonetheless respect the demarcation between the full original jurisdiction conferred on the High Court by Article 34.3.1⁰ on the one hand, and the "local and limited" nature of the Circuit Court's Article 34.3.4⁰ jurisdiction on the other. This means in turn that the latter Court "may not be erected into a localised replica of the High Court": see JP Casey, "The Constitution and the Legal System" (1979) 14 Irish Jurist 14 at 18. 

 8.       As matters stand, it is clear from the provisions of the Third Schedule to the Courts (Supplemental Provisions) Act 1961, that jurisdiction is exercised locally, in that the Circuit Court can only hear cases against defendants residing in or carrying on business in or arising out of events happening in or immoveable property situate in, the Circuit in question.  But what is the status of these orders outside of the Circuit (or, in the case of the District Court, the relevant District) in which they are made? 

 9.       While it might be thought that there is a surprising dearth of authority on this point, it seems to me as a matter of principle that once the Circuit Court sitting in Circuit A has personal jurisdiction over a particular defendant (by reason, for example, of the fact that the defendant carries on business within that Circuit), it can then make an order in personam against that defendant, which can take effect outside of the jurisdiction of that Court. This simply reflects the complete nature of the personal jurisdiction which the Circuit Court enjoys over the defendant once these jurisdictional requirements specified in the 1961 Act have been satisfied. So, for example, if Circuit Court A makes a monetary award against a particular defendant, it would be entitled in principle to make a consequential Mareva -type order restraining that defendant from reducing his or her assets below a specified amount anywhere in the State (assuming, of course, that the substantive requirements of that Mareva jurisdiction have otherwise been satisfied). 

 10.   What the Circuit Court could not do, however, is to make an order in rem which takes effect outside of its jurisdiction. If, for example, the Circuit Court in Circuit A were to make a monetary award against X, it would not itself have jurisdiction to make a well-charging order against immoveable property situate in Circuit B in the event that this award remained undischarged. In those circumstances, it would be necessary to apply to the Circuit Court sitting in Circuit B for this relief. 

 11.    The reason for this distinction is that an in rem order of this kind applies indistinctly and indifferently to all persons and things who or which might be affected by its terms. If, for example, the Circuit Court were to make such a well-charging order in respect of immovable property situate outside of its Circuit, this would be tantamount to that Court acquiring a substantive jurisdiction to make orders in rem as against the entire world in respect of such property, which jurisdiction it would not otherwise possess. Not only has the Court not been given jurisdiction in respect of immoveable property situate outside of its own Circuit, but such an order might affect the rights of other persons not otherwise amenable to the jurisdiction of that Court. 

 12.    If one applies this principle to the Isaac Wunder jurisdiction at issue in the present case, it will be seen that the Circuit Court (and, by extension, the District Court) can make such an order in personam as against the offending litigant in respect of the litigation in which the Court has seisin, and in respect of which it already has personal jurisdiction over the party concerned. If, for example, X sues Y in Circuit Court A because this is the jurisdiction in which Y resides, then Circuit Court A can, where appropriate, make an Isaac Wunder order restraining X from suing Y in the Circuit Court anywhere in the State without prior leave. This, in essence, is the grant of ancillary relief to one of the parties in respect of litigation of which the court has jurisdiction and is properly seised. 

 13.    This jurisdiction does not, however, enable the Circuit Court to make an in rem Isaac Wunder order which would take effect generally in respect of other litigation and other parties outside of that particular Circuit. It could not, for instance, in the example I have just given, make an order which would restrain X from suing any other person in another Circuit without prior leave, since that would amount in substance to that Circuit Court exercising a general jurisdiction in respect of other parties and other litigation and in respect of parties and matters over which it does not enjoy such a jurisdiction. 

 Conclusions 

 14.   Subject to these observations, I agree with the judgment of Dunne J. that this appeal should be dismissed. I consider that the jurisdiction to make an Isaac Wunder order is ultimately derived from the courts' Article 34.1 obligation to conserve and protect the administration of justice. 

 15.   While the Circuit Court can in principle make an Isaac Wunder order in personam in respect of a party over which it has acquired personal jurisdiction which takes effect outside of that Circuit, that does not enable the Circuit Court to make an in rem Isaac Wunder order which would take effect generally outside of that Circuit which restrains that litigant from suing other parties in respect of which that Court does not have personal jurisdiction.
